content.text: A tool isn't an API client for Claude. Every definition and every response lands in the model's limited context, and the caller decides what to do next from what it reads. Tools that mirror endpoints one by one make Claude page through lists, chain calls and juggle raw IDs. Design tools around the tasks people actually ask for, return only what the next step needs, and describe each one the way you'd brief a new colleague.

A support team connects Claude to the company CRM with a generator that turns the OpenAPI spec into tools, one per endpoint. Coverage looks complete. Then a teammate asks, "Why was Dana Levi charged twice in March?" Claude pages through

looking for Dana, pulls her entire transaction history, then the notes, and after a dozen calls full of UUIDs it reports a refund that belongs to a different customer. Every endpoint worked. The tools still failed.
"Wrapping each existing API endpoint as a tool, with a short description, is good tool design for Claude." It's how we've always integrated systems:

items.text: A client library mirrors the API it calls, so a tool set that mirrors the API feels just as correct.
Generators turn an OpenAPI file into tools in minutes, and full coverage feels thorough.
The endpoints are already tested, documented and permissioned, so reusing them seems safest.
More tools sound like more capability.

content.text: The half-truth: calling your existing API from a tool is fine, and often the right implementation. The mistake is copying the API's
, one route per tool, into the interface the model sees.
A tool is a contract with a non-deterministic caller

Anthropic's engineering guide on writing tools puts it this way: "Tools are a new kind of software which reflects a contract between deterministic systems and non-deterministic agents." Given "Should I bring an umbrella today?", an agent might call the weather tool, answer from general knowledge or ask where you are. So the guide's advice is to stop writing tools "the way we'd write functions and APIs for other developers or systems" and design them for
Your API's usual consumers are programs, and for them memory is cheap: looping over thousands of rows is trivial. An agent reads every returned token inside its
. The guide's example is an address book: a
tool forces the agent to read contacts one by one, like reading the address book from the first page. A
tool lets it jump to the right page. And whatever the tool returns stays in the conversation, re-sent with every later turn.
Shape tools around tasks, not routes

The guide names the mistake directly: "A common error we've observed is tools that merely wrap existing software functionality or API endpoints." Its alternatives consolidate what agents otherwise chain:

items.text: schedule_event
, which finds availability and books, instead of
list_users
list_events
and
create_event
search_logs
, which returns relevant lines with some context, instead of
read_logs
get_customer_context
, which compiles a customer's recent, relevant information, instead of
get_customer_by_id
list_transactions
and
list_notes

content.text: Claude's tool docs say the same: "Fewer, more capable tools reduce selection ambiguity," and when tools span services, prefix them with the service name, such as
Return what the next step needs
Responses should carry "only high signal information." The guide suggests dropping low-level fields such as
, and reports that resolving arbitrary UUIDs to meaningful names "significantly improves Claude's precision in retrieval tasks by reducing hallucinations." When a later call needs an ID, a

options lets the agent ask for it. Large results get pagination, filtering or truncation with sensible defaults, and errors should say what to change instead of returning an opaque code or a traceback.
Here's the generated tool set next to one tool built for the question people actually ask:

# Generated from openapi.yaml: one tool per endpoint
TOOLS = [
    {"name": "get_customers", "description": "GET /customers",
     "input_schema": {"type": "object",
                      "properties": {"page": {"type": "integer"}}}},
    {"name": "get_customer_transactions",
     "description": "GET /customers/{id}/transactions",
     "input_schema": {"type": "object",
                      "properties": {"id": {"type": "string"}},
                      "required": ["id"]}},
    {"name": "get_customer_notes",
     "description": "GET /customers/{id}/notes",
     "input_schema": {"type": "object",
                      "properties": {"id": {"type": "string"}},
                      "required": ["id"]}},
    # ...and one more for every other route in the spec
]

tabs.label: ✅ Right

content.text: The implementation still calls the same REST API; the difference is what reaches the model:

blocks.code:
def crm_get_customer_context(customer: str, response_format="concise"):
    matches = crm.search_customers(customer, limit=5)  # never the full list
    if len(matches) != 1:
        found = "; ".join(f"{m.name} <{m.email}>" for m in matches) or "none"
        return f"{len(matches)} matches for {customer!r}: {found}. Ask which."
    c = matches[0]
    lines = [f"{c.name} <{c.email}>, customer since {c.since}"]
    lines += [f"{t.date} {t.amount} {t.status}"
              for t in crm.list_transactions(c.id, limit=20)]
    lines += [f"note: {n.text}" for n in crm.list_notes(c.id, status="open")]
    if response_format == "detailed":  # IDs only when a next call needs them
        lines.append(f"customer_id: {c.id}")
    return "\n".join(lines)


print(crm_get_customer_context("Dana Levi"))

content.text: One call answers the question that took a dozen. The two March charges sit next to each other under Dana's name, with no UUIDs to mix up, and an ambiguous name produces a short list and an instruction instead of a guess.

blocks.title: More tools can make Claude worse

content.text: Tool definitions are sent with every request, and the guide warns that "too many tools or overlapping tools can also distract agents from pursuing efficient strategies." Dozens of near-identical getters cost context on every call and give Claude more ways to pick the wrong one.

blocks.title: Measure tools the way you'd measure a model

content.text: The guide's process is evaluation-driven: write realistic tasks that need several tool calls, run them in a simple agent loop, and track accuracy, tool calls, tokens and errors. Lots of redundant calls point to pagination limits; lots of invalid-parameter errors point to unclear descriptions.
How to apply it in your project
Collect the questions people really ask your assistant, from logs or support tickets, and design one tool per frequent workflow.
If the agent always calls three tools in a row, make one tool that does all three against your API.
Give every collection a search with filters, a small default limit and a hint when results are truncated.
